title: Mechanical Waves — 50 MCQs
description: 50 questions covering speed of wave motion, velocity of sound in solids, liquids and gases, Laplace correction, effects of temperature/pressure/humidity, and numerical problems.

questions.q: Which is the best definition of a mechanical wave?
options: A disturbance that transfers energy through a medium without net transport of matter
A flow of fluid that transports mass
questions.explanation: Mechanical waves are disturbances that transfer energy through a material medium while individual particles oscillate about equilibrium positions.

questions.q: The relation between angular frequency ω, wave number k and wave speed v for a progressive wave is:
questions.explanation: For a sinusoidal progressive wave, phase velocity v = ω/k.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes longitudinal and transverse mechanical waves?
options: Longitudinal: occurs only in solids; Transverse: occurs only in gases
Longitudinal: particle motion along propagation; Transverse: particle motion perpendicular to propagation
Longitudinal: no energy transfer; Transverse: transfers energy
questions.explanation: Longitudinal waves have particle displacements parallel to propagation (e.g. sound); transverse waves have displacements perpendicular.

questions.q: Speed of small-amplitude longitudinal waves in a liquid is given by:
questions.explanation: For liquids, v = √(bulk modulus K divided by density ρ).

questions.q: Speed of longitudinal (elastic) waves in a solid rod (approx.) is often expressed as:
questions.explanation: A commonly used approximation for longitudinal waves in a thin rod uses Young's modulus E: v ≈ √(E/ρ).

questions.q: The speed of sound in an ideal gas (adiabatic) is:
questions.explanation: Adiabatic speed of sound in a gas: v = √(γ R T / M) where γ is ratio of specific heats, R the gas constant, T absolute temperature, M molar mass.

questions.q: Laplace correction in the speed of sound accounts for:
options: The adiabatic nature of sound waves
questions.explanation: Laplace showed that compressions are essentially adiabatic for sound; the correction replaces isothermal relation with an adiabatic factor γ, increasing predicted speed.

questions.q: How does temperature (T) of a gas affect speed of sound (all else constant)?
questions.explanation: For ideal gas v = √(γ R T / M), so v ∝ √T; increasing absolute temperature increases speed.

questions.q: Humidity (increasing water vapour fraction) typically affects speed of sound in air by:
options: Slightly increasing speed because moist air has lower mean molecular mass
questions.explanation: Water vapour has lower molar mass than dry air, reducing mean molecular mass and increasing sound speed slightly.

questions.q: For an ideal gas at constant temperature, increasing pressure changes the speed of sound how?
options: Little or no change (speed depends on temperature, not pressure)
questions.explanation: At constant temperature for an ideal gas, speed v = √(γ P/ρ) with ρ proportional to P, so P/ρ = RT/M constant — speed depends on T, not P.

questions.q: Using the approximate empirical relation v ≈ 331 + 0.6 T(°C), speed of sound in dry air at 20°C is about:
questions.explanation: Plugging T=20°C gives v ≈ 331 + 0.6×20 = 343 m/s (approx.).

questions.q: If frequency of a sound wave is 1000 Hz and speed in medium is 343 m/s, the wavelength is:
Time period T of a wave whose frequency is 500 Hz is:
If absolute temperature of an ideal gas doubles, the speed of sound (approximately) becomes:
questions.explanation: v ∝ √T, so doubling T increases speed by factor √2.

questions.q: Holding elastic modulus constant, what is effect of increasing density on wave speed in a solid?
questions.explanation: For v ≈ √(E/ρ), increasing ρ reduces v (inverse square-root dependence).

questions.q: The bulk modulus K has SI units of:
questions.explanation: Bulk modulus is pressure-like (stress/strain) and has units of pressure, Pa.

questions.q: Young's modulus E (used in solid wave speed approximations) has units:
questions.explanation: Young's modulus is stress/strain ratio, units of pressure: Pascal.

questions.q: Estimate longitudinal wave speed in steel: E ≈ 2.0×10¹¹ Pa, ρ ≈ 7800 kg/m³. Closest value is:
Estimate speed of sound in water: bulk modulus K ≈ 2.2×10⁹ Pa, ρ ≈ 1000 kg/m³. Closest value:
For diatomic gases (like dry air) γ (Cp/Cv) is approximately:
questions.explanation: Diatomic gases at room temperature typically have γ ≈ 1.4 (rotational modes active).

questions.q: Laplace correction changes the isothermal formula v = √(R T / M) to the adiabatic form by multiplying under the root by:
questions.explanation: Laplace correction: use adiabatic exponent γ, giving v = √(γ R T / M).

questions.q: Ideal gas relation connecting pressure P, density ρ and temperature T is:
questions.explanation: P = ρ R_specific T, where R_specific = R/M; so P = ρ (R/M) T.

questions.q: Estimate speed of sound in helium at 27°C assuming γ=1.66, M=0.004 kg/mol, R=8.314 J/mol·K (T≈300 K). Closest value:
Using v = √(γ R T / M), estimate speed of sound in dry air (γ=1.4, M≈0.029 kg/mol) at 20°C (T=293 K). Closest:
questions.explanation: Compute v ≈ √(1.4×8.314×293/0.029) ≈ 343 m/s (standard value).

questions.q: For two media with acoustic impedances Z1 and Z2, larger mismatch causes:
options: More reflection and less transmission at the interface
questions.explanation: Reflection coefficient depends on impedance mismatch; greater mismatch → larger reflection.

questions.q: Acoustic impedance Z of a medium is defined as:
questions.explanation: Acoustic impedance Z = ρ × c (density times sound speed).

questions.q: Approximate acoustic impedance of water (ρ≈1000 kg/m³, c≈1480 m/s) is:
Intensity I of a wave (in a medium) is proportional to:
questions.explanation: Acoustic intensity ∝ amplitude²; exact relation depends on medium (I ∝ p_rms²/(ρ c) or ∝ ρ c ω² A²/2 for displacement amplitude A).

questions.q: A sound wave of frequency 1000 Hz in air (v=343 m/s) has wavelength:
Group velocity equals phase velocity when the medium is:
questions.explanation: In non-dispersive media (ω proportional to k), group velocity = phase velocity.

questions.q: Dispersion in a medium means:
questions.explanation: Dispersion: different frequency components travel at different phase velocities.

questions.q: Which formula gives the Doppler-shifted frequency f' for a moving source approaching a stationary observer (source speed u, wave speed v)?
questions.explanation: For source moving towards observer f' = f v / (v - u).

questions.q: A source emits sound of 1000 Hz and approaches observer at 30 m/s. If v=343 m/s, approximate observed frequency is:
Reflection of sound from a rigid boundary typically produces at the boundary:
questions.explanation: A rigid wall enforces zero particle displacement, which corresponds to a pressure antinode (maximum pressure fluctuation) at the boundary.

questions.q: Viscous absorption and thermal conduction in a medium cause:
questions.explanation: Viscous and thermal effects dissipate wave energy, causing attenuation (amplitude decay) with distance.

questions.q: The dominant factor determining sound speed in gases under normal conditions is:
questions.explanation: For ideal gases at normal conditions, speed depends primarily on absolute temperature (and molecular composition).

questions.q: If the molecular weight of the gas decreases (keeping T constant), the speed of sound:
questions.explanation: v = √(γ R T / M) so lower molar mass M increases v.

questions.q: An approximation often used for speed of sound in dry air as function of temperature °C is:
questions.explanation: Empirical linear approximation around room temperature: v ≈ 331 + 0.6 T°C.

questions.q: If sound intensity level is 60 dB, the corresponding intensity (I) is:
questions.explanation: Reference intensity I₀ = 1×10⁻¹² W/m²; level L=10 log₁₀(I/I₀). For L=60 dB, I = I₀×10^(60/10)=1e-12×1e6=1e-6 W/m².

questions.q: Percent increase in speed of sound when replacing isothermal formula by adiabatic using γ=1.4 is approximately:
questions.explanation: Factor = √γ = √1.4 ≈ 1.183 → ~18.3% increase compared to isothermal value.

questions.q: Which of the following factors typically causes the largest change in speed of sound in air?
options: Temperature change of several tens of °C
Small change in pressure at fixed T
questions.explanation: Temperature has the largest effect on speed of sound in air; pressure at fixed T does not change speed.

questions.q: Energy carried by a progressive mechanical wave is transported:
options: In the direction of wave propagation (on average)
questions.explanation: Progressive waves transport energy through the medium in the direction of wave propagation.

questions.q: Which expression gives wavelength λ when angular frequency ω and wave speed v are known?
questions.explanation: k = ω/v and k = 2π/λ, so λ = 2π v / ω.

questions.q: For a non-dispersive mechanical wave packet, which statement is true?
options: Wave packet shape does not change while traveling
questions.explanation: In non-dispersive media all frequencies travel at same speed so packet preserves shape (ignoring attenuation).

questions.q: Stokes' assumption about sound propagation in gases (Laplace correction) implies compressions are:
questions.explanation: Laplace recognized compressions/expansions during sound propagation are too fast to exchange heat, so they are essentially adiabatic.

questions.q: Which phenomenon explains why sound travels faster in warm air than in cold air?
options: Increased average molecular speed (higher T) raising pressure to density ratio
questions.explanation: Higher absolute temperature increases thermal energy and the factor RT/M, increasing v ≈ √(γ R T / M).

questions.q: Longitudinal wave speed in a bulk isotropic solid (exact expression) depends on bulk modulus K and shear modulus G as:
questions.explanation: General formula for longitudinal wave speed in a solid involves both bulk and shear moduli: v = √((K + 4G/3)/ρ).
